name: Rayleigh–Taylor instability
question: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?

derived.label: grid
derived.note: coefficients are in grid units, so the physical experiment changes with resolution

plots.title: Mixing width
plots.explain: Height fraction where the horizontally averaged scalar, normalised by its initial heavy and light values, lies between 0.1 and 0.9. The unmixed initial state therefore has near-zero width. Classical theory gives h ≈ α A g t² late in the mixing regime; this run uses a constant-density projection with density only in the buoyancy term (a Boussinesq-like approximation), so quantitative growth rates at high Atwood number are not established here.

ns_rt_single.name: Rayleigh–Taylor, Single Mode
ns_rt_single.question: Can the early growth of one interface mode be measured consistently?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: Can the early growth of one interface mode be measured consistently?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A single small-amplitude cosine ripple with two wavelengths across the box. One bubble and one spike per wavelength grow before the nonlinear mushroom stage.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Change the wavenumber (1–4) and compare how fast the mixing width starts to grow.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The early, near-exponential part of the mixing-width curve.
more: Repeat at a higher resolution to check the early growth is resolution-independent.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
Put a dense fluid on top of a lighter one in gravity and the configuration stores potential energy it 'wants' to release by overturning. It is unstable to the smallest perturbation: a tiny dip in the interface lets heavy fluid poke down into light fluid, where it is even less supported, so the dip grows. Heavy fluid falls in narrow spikes; light fluid rises in broad bubbles.

As a spike accelerates through the lighter fluid it shears against it, and that shear is itself Kelvin–Helmholtz unstable — so the tip of each spike curls over into the iconic mushroom cap, and the caps in turn shed smaller vortices. The flow thus couples a large-scale buoyant overturning to a cascade of smaller shear instabilities, which is why it mixes so efficiently.

The Rayleigh–Taylor instability is everywhere there is acceleration across a density jump: the expanding remnants of supernovae, the compression of fuel in inertial-confinement fusion, rising salt domes in geology, and overturning in the oceans and atmosphere.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• u, ∂t u + (u·∇)u, −∇p, ν∇²u, ∇·u=0 — the incompressible Navier–Stokes terms
• −g·ρ·ŷ — the gravitational body force; heavier fluid (larger ρ) is pulled down harder, which is the source of the instability
• ρ here is an advected density field carried with the flow
• A = (ρ_heavy − ρ_light)/(ρ_heavy + ρ_light) — the Atwood number sets the density contrast across the interface; the spike growth rate scales like √(A·g·k), so higher A gives faster, narrower fingers

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Heavy over light with a single cosine ripple of the chosen wavenumber and small amplitude (2 % of the height); at rest.
layers.bc: Closed no-penetration top and bottom; free-slip side walls.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: The same constant-density projection solver with an advected scalar ρ that enters only the gravitational body force (a Boussinesq-like approximation: inertia does not change with density). The interface is seeded with a multi-mode ripple, or a single mode of chosen wavenumber.
layers.checks: Numerical check (consistency across resolutions); the linear growth rate is not compared with theory because the model is Boussinesq-like and viscous.

layers.title: References
items: Sharp, D.H. (1984). An overview of Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Physica D 12, 3–18.

ns_rt.name: Rayleigh–Taylor Fingers
ns_rt.question: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: Heavy fluid rests on light fluid in gravity. The interface is unstable: spikes fall, bubbles rise, and each finger rolls up into a mushroom cap.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Open the Single-Mode scene to measure the early growth of one wavelength.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The mixing-layer width versus time (normalised by the initial heavy/light values).
more: Change the Atwood number from 0.2 to 1.0 and compare the mixing-width curves.

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Heavy fluid resting on light fluid, separated by a small multi-mode interface ripple; everything at rest.
layers.bc: Closed, no-penetration top and bottom; free-slip side walls — a sealed box.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: The same constant-density projection solver with an advected scalar ρ that enters only the gravitational body force (a Boussinesq-like approximation: inertia does not change with density). The interface is seeded with a multi-mode ripple, or a single mode of chosen wavenumber.
layers.checks: Qualitative demonstration: density only enters the buoyancy force of a constant-density projection solver (a Boussinesq-like approximation). Quantitative large-Atwood growth rates need a variable-density formulation and are not claimed.

layers.title: References
items: Sharp, D.H. (1984). An overview of Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Physica D 12, 3–18.

atwood.label: Atwood number
atwood.help: A = (ρ_heavy − ρ_light)/(ρ_heavy + ρ_light), the density contrast across the interface. Higher A → faster, narrower spikes. (Boussinesq-like model: density only enters the buoyancy force; see the scene notes.)

gravity.label: Gravity
gravity.help: Gravity driving the instability. Higher → faster fingering / collapse.

viscosity.label: Viscosity
viscosity.help: Kinematic viscosity ν — how 'thick' the fluid is. Lower → finer, more chaotic structures; higher → smoother, damped flow.

perturbation.label: Interface ripple
perturbation.help: Amplitude of the initial interface ripple that seeds the fingers.

modes.label: Single-mode wavenumber
modes.help: 0 = the multi-mode ripple (modes 3 + 7). A value n ≥ 1 seeds a single cosine mode with n wavelengths across the box and a small amplitude, for measuring the early growth of one mode.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
